payload.author: Juan Lentino
payload.content:
The generative tools have started signing their outputs. An image, and from some vendors an audio render, leaves the service with a sealed credential naming the model, the vendor, and the moment, and the reflex reading is that the provenance problem has begun solving itself: the machines are labeling the machines. The credential is real and worth having. What it asserts is much narrower than the relief suggests, and the difference deserves a close look before anyone builds policy on it.

A generative tool can attest only to its own output

A service signing its own output can attest to exactly what it observed: this file left this system at this moment, produced under this account. Those are facts, sealed by a party in a position to know them, and they do useful work.

A distributor can check whether a delivered master matches a generator's output record. A court can establish that a file existed inside a vendor's logs on a date. The facts are also hard to get any other way, since the vendor's logs are the only place they ever existed. The tool is a competent witness to its own participation.

Participation is where its knowledge ends. The service cannot see whose hands drove it or how much of the result the person shaped. It also cannot see what it never touched: the session before the prompt and the session after the render are both outside the frame. A render that became one texture inside a forty-track production and a render uploaded whole carry the same credential. The tool's testimony covers the tool.

A witness is not an author

Read correctly, the self-signed credential is an input-layer record, one voice in the stack rather than a verdict about the work. It belongs beside the signed loop and the signed stem, inputs signed at the layer that made them, feeding a record that some human eventually has to top with a claim of their own.

The credential's most useful property may be what it makes visible by contrast. A delivery full of signed tool records and no signed human claim is now a legible shape, and silence in a field that could have carried a claim reads differently than silence where no field existed. Distributor intake that starts requiring tool credentials would make that human silence louder still, and pressure of that kind is probably where this layer's adoption actually comes from.

One distributor has already drawn that line for a single generator. In April, Believe began blocking distribution of tracks made on unlicensed AI platforms through Believe and TuneCore, and in September it made every track created with Suno's new industry-partner model eligible, under a deal that puts participating Believe and TuneCore repertoire into that model's training. The announcement does not say whether those deliveries carry a credential from the tool.

Believe announced the block on April 30, 2026, and the Suno partnership on September 8.

The vendor testifies about itself

The credential is also the vendor's testimony about the vendor, which is a category to hold carefully. The signer profits from the service being trusted and decides unilaterally what its credentials say. It can change the policy or the meaning next quarter. Whether the attestation service keeps behaving as described is not a question a signature answers; it is the other of the two kinds of provenance, the behavioral kind, where the answer can move.

The credential verifies forever, while the trustworthiness behind it is a subscription. Reading a tool credential from 2026 in 2031 means asking what the vendor's signing policy was then, a research task the file itself cannot carry. A catalog that leans on tool credentials has taken a position on a company's future conduct, whether it meant to or not.

None of which makes the machine's admission worthless. It makes it the cheapest claim in the file: the machine stating it is a machine, a fact nobody was going to contest. The expensive claim, the one disputes are actually about, is the human one, and no tool can make it on a person's behalf. The self-signing generator has not solved authorship. It has cleared the stage of the one question that was never hard.

References

OpenAI. "Provenance signals (Content Credentials, SynthID) in OpenAI-generated content." OpenAI Help Center. Accessed October 2026. help.openai.com

ElevenLabs. "Compose music." API reference, sign_with_c2pa parameter. Accessed October 2026. elevenlabs.io

Believe. "Believe and Suno announce strategic partnership to advance licensed AI music opportunities for independent artists and labels." September 8, 2026. believe.com

Music Business Worldwide. "Suno inks global licensing deal with Believe." September 2026. musicbusinessworldwide.com
payload.title: When the tool signs itself
